Chapter 4: Power, Truth, and the Making of History
Every society shares stories about itself. These stories shape how you see the world, how you find your place in it, and even what you believe is possible. But have you ever wondered—are all stories treated the same? Some get amplified and repeated, making their way into textbooks, while others are quietly pushed aside, distorted, or even erased.
It’s not accidental. The decision about which stories matter is often a reflection of power—plain and simple.
Think back to your school days. In so many classrooms, the version of history you learn usually reflects the interests of those who’ve held power. There’s a celebration of some groups’ achievements, while the contributions of others barely get a mention, if at all. And this isn’t just a simple oversight. It’s a conscious choice—one that quietly keeps old hierarchies in place.
Maybe you—or someone you know—have looked at a history book and noticed key stories missing. Or wondered why certain events are called “discoveries,” when people were already living there. When you ask these questions, the answers often feel hollow. What you’re really running up against is the edge of the official narrative.
History isn’t just a straightforward record. It’s a process of picking and choosing—deciding which events are important, who gets to be a hero, and what stories are worth telling. And those choices? They’re shaped by the values and interests of people in positions of power. So, the version of the past that feels “natural” is actually the result of careful curation.
The impact of this selective storytelling runs deep. When certain histories are erased, it becomes easier to justify inequality. When the achievements—and struggles—of marginalized groups are ignored, it’s as if they’re invisible. The stories we tell don’t just shape how we see the past; they influence how we imagine the future, too.
But here’s the good news: history isn’t set in stone. It’s always being rewritten, challenged, and reimagined. All across the world, people are working to recover lost stories, to question the old narratives, and to create new ways of understanding the past.
This work isn’t easy. It means facing up to uncomfortable truths, rethinking beliefs you may have held for years, and really seeing how power shapes what we know. It takes an open mind—a willingness to listen to those who’ve been silenced, and to view the world from a different angle.
In schools, more teachers are bringing in new materials, encouraging real critical thinking, and making space for voices that haven’t always been heard. In communities, elders are passing down stories that might have otherwise faded away. And at home, parents are teaching kids to question what they hear and to search for the truth themselves.
The journey to reclaim history is ongoing. It’s a shared effort—a collective project that calls for curiosity, courage, and persistence. It’s about recognizing just how powerful storytelling really is, and using that power to build a world that’s more just and inclusive for everyone.
